catalog_quote: 2.2.4. Zuberoan. Zuberoan is the only eastern dialect with contrastive accent. The general accentual rule of Zuberoan is penultimate accent, as seen in table 40. [Table 40. Zuberoan: General paroxytonic pattern: gízun 'man', gizúna 'the man, ABS', gizúnak 'the men, ABS or the man, ERG'; bezála 'like', bezaláko '(of) like', bezalakóxe '(of) like, DIM'] However, there is also a marked oxytonic pattern. In some cases, oxytonic accent is clearly the result of a historical contraction. For instance, the absolutive singular form of stems ending in -a, where a historical sequence /a+a/ has been reduced, shows final accent, table 41 (a). Final accent is also found in plural forms of all words, except in the absolutive. To explain this case a historical contraction has also been proposed, table 41 (b). [Table 41. Zuberoan: Exceptional oxytonic pattern: (a) alhabá 'the daughter, ABS' < *alhaba-a,…
sweep_summary: Basque (basq1248, catalog classification lexical, deciding source Hualde 2003 sec. 2.2.4 Zuberoan). 24 title hits: 9 are other languages or general theory (Clemens, Eychenne, Leben, Melvold, Enguehard, Wagner, Nouveau, Boukous, Hammond). The 15 Basque items are almost all Hualde's De Gruyter/Benjamins/Elsevier papers (1993 Getxo, 1993 Diachronica, 1996 reconstruction, 1998 Azkoitia, 1999 'Basque accentuation', 2000 Markina, 2002 dialectology, 2002 LabPhon pitch-to-stress [Glottolog lists it twice], 2003 western shift, 2007 convergence) — all paywalled (De Gruyter serves only a bot challenge; ScienceDirect 403); only the Diachronica abstract was reachable ('in a large central area there is no contrastive word accent, systems with phonologically distinctive accentuation are found both in eastern and western regions'). downloaded and read: Elordieta & Selkirk 2018 (open, UCSC festschrift) — Lekeitio Northern Bizkaian has a lexical accented/unaccented contrast with the HL accent fixed on the penultimate of accented words; confirms the lexical coding for a western variety. Ito 2002 (UIUC) is on IDEALS but its PDF is access-restricted (abstract only; focus intonation in Bermeo Basque, not placement). Aurrekoetxea et al. 2012 'Stress areas' (LimiAr proceedings) and the undated Hualde Souletin manuscript could not be located. Best first-hand statement read: the held Hualde 1997 monograph sec. 4.2-4.3 (Zuberoan penultimate by rule with lexically marked oxytones), which confirms and does not supersede the catalog's Hualde 2003 passage. Highest-priority unread item remains Hualde 1999 'Basque accentuation' (van der Hulst vol.). Bing returned junk), so 'not found' items had only Crossref, Glottolog, IDEALS and publisher pages behind them.

Azentuera hau Zuberoa eta Erronkaritik Baztan eta Ultzamaraino hedatzen da. [...] Hauetariko hizkera batzuetan, hala nola zubereraz eta, batez ere, erronkarieraz, salbuespen lexiko eta morfologikoek azentuzko bereizketak sortzen dituzte. [...] Zubereraz, azentua normalean azkenaurreko silaban ezartzen da. [...] Hitz guztiek, hala ere, ez dute patroi hau erakusten. Batzuetan azentua azken silaban doa. Hasteko, benetako salbuespen lexikoak ditugu
new_statements.translation: In a wide eastern region the accent generally goes on the penultimate syllable; that is, the main rule is [-2]. This accentuation extends from Zuberoa and Erronkari to Baztan and Ultzama. [...] In some of these varieties, such as Zuberoan and above all Roncalese, lexical and morphological exceptions create accentual contrasts. [...] In Zuberoan the accent is normally placed on the penultimate syllable. [...] Not all words show this pattern, however. Sometimes the accent goes on the final syllable. To begin with, we have genuine lexical exceptions
new_statements.citation: Hualde, José Ignacio. 1997. Euskararen azentuerak (ASJUren Gehigarriak 42). Donostia/Bilbo: Gipuzkoako Foru Aldundia & UPV/EHU. DOI 10.1387/asju.8621 (open, ASJU OJS). Ch. 4 'Ekialdeko azentubidea', sec. 4.2 (p. 74) and sec. 4.3.1 'Zuberoa: azentu patroiak flexiogabeko oinarrietan' (pp. 75-76).
new_statements.reading: Hualde's own fullest treatment: the eastern type (Zuberoan included) is penultimate by rule, with a class of lexically marked oxytones (arrés, andé, etc.), plus predictable finals in glide-final and nasal-vowel-final words and after lexically accented monosyllabic suffixes (-ñi, -tiar, -kor). Read from the held scanned; '[-2] da' normalises the scanned garble '~2] cia'. This is the same description the catalog's deciding 2003 passage condenses and it confirms the 'lexical' coding for Zuberoan (penultimate default + marked oxytonic pattern). Among items actually read this search of works with stress in the title, Elordieta & Selkirk 2018 adds the Lekeitio (Northern Bizkaian) lexical accented/unaccented contrast with fixed penultimate placement in accented words.

new_statements.quote: This thesis investigates how the informational status of words is expressed by means of intonation in two pitch accent languages, Tokyo Japanese and Bermeo Basuque, in which the tonal shape of words is lexically determined. [...] The focal status of a word did not affect the alignment of the pitch peak of a lexical accent in a consistent manner in either Tokyo Japanese or Bermeo Basque.
new_statements.citation: Ito, Kiwako (2002). The Interaction of Focus and Lexical Pitch Accent in Speech Production and Dialogue Comprehension: Evidence from Japanese and Basque. PhD dissertation, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (chair: Jennifer Cole). IDEALS record hdl.handle.net/2142/82617. [Glottolog 624612]
new_statements.locator: IDEALS record page, Abstract field (file itself restricted: 'This item is only available for download by members of the University of Illinois community')
new_statements.relation_note: Describes the Bermeo (Northern Bizkaian) variety as a lexical pitch accent system; compatible with the existing statement's remark on the Lekeitio accented/unaccented contrast and with the eastern penultimate-plus-lexical-oxytones description, which concerns a different dialect group. Abstract only; the dissertation body could not be opened (UIUC NetID required, not reachable by automated download/403 then record page 200 with a browser UA).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bermeo (Northern Bizkaian) Basque is treated as a lexical pitch accent language: the tonal shape of a word is lexically specified and focus raises pitch without moving the lexical accent peak. The abstract gives no placement rule.
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog entry is 'Basque' with an empty rule; every usable statement is dialect-specific. Existing statement (Hualde 1997): eastern type, Zuberoan/Souletin and Roncalese to Baztan/Ultzama. Ito 2002: Bermeo, Northern Bizkaian (pitch accent). de Rijk 1972: Gipuzkoan (central) Basque, with Michelena's remark covering the central and western dialects generally and explicitly noting that even Souletin versification ignores the accent. Hualde 1999 (unopened) is the WALS source for eleven separate Basque doculects (Bidasoa Valley, Gernika, Hondarribia, Basaburua-Imoz, Lekeitio, Northern High Navarrese, Oñati, Roncalese, Sakana, Zeberio, Souletin), which signals that a single stress value for basq1250 is a simplification.

new_statements.quote: Intonational phenomena in Guipúzcoan Basque are elusive in the extreme. No one knows what the system of rules for stress assignment looks like; to date, not even observational adequacy has been achieved. The difficulty is partly that the intonation can be markedly different in neighboring villages all over the area, [...] and partly that stressed syllables have very little acoustic prominence over the others, as contrasted with the stressed syllables of Spanish, English or Russian. (p. 21) [...] Second, in relativized present tense forms, where there is no underlying double final consonant, as a rule we also find final stress (p. 22)
new_statements.citation: de Rijk, Rudolph P. G. (1972). Studies in Basque Syntax: Relative Clauses. Massachusetts Inst. of Technology. MIT. ix+182 pp.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2, section 'Relative Clauses and Stress', pp. 20-25 (PDF pp. 29-34), quotes from pp. 21-22 (PDF pp. 30-31), checked against the page images; footnote 4 p. 62 (PDF p. 71)
new_statements.relation_note: Describes a different dialect (Gipuzkoan, central Basque) from the eastern penultimate-with-lexical-oxytones system in the existing Hualde 1997 statement, so it neither agrees nor contradicts on placement; it adds that in the central dialect word stress is weakly realised, has no known rule as of 1972, and that relativized verb forms carry final stress. The listed MPG open_url (pure.mpg.de item_403085) is IP-restricted (401 'does not match required ip range'); the copy read is the MIT DSpace scan (hdl 1721.1/12980), which has no text layer and was scanned at 200 dpi.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Gipuzkoan (central) Basque the author says no stress-assignment rule is known, that stress varies village by village, and that stressed syllables are only weakly prominent; the one regularity he states is final stress on relativized verb forms (both past and present tense, e.g. zutén, dutén, zetorrén), with occasional exceptions and with non-relativized forms also sometimes taking final stress. He quotes Michelena (Fonética Histórica Vasca, p. 379) that in the central and western dialects the differences of intensity, pitch and duration between syllables are small and hard to perceive and 'El valor distintivo del acento es por otra parte reducido' ('The phonemic value of the accent is, on the other hand, rather small').
new_statements.exceptions: 'while final stress in relativized verb forms is certainly the rule, exceptions (i.e. cases where the final stress is not physically realized) do ocasionally occur. Fourth, with even greater frequency, it happens that non-relativized verb forms too get final stress.' (p. 23). Fn. 4 (p. 62) speculates that final stress was originally limited to past-tense relativized forms and spread to present-tense forms by analogy. Also p. 154: 'there is no difference in intonation between restrictive and appositive relative clauses in Basque.'

readall_conflicts: No source opened contradicts another on the same variety, but the sources describe different dialects and give different prosodic types: the existing Hualde 1997 statement gives the eastern (Zuberoan/Roncalese) type as penultimate by rule with lexically marked oxytones; the Ito 2002 abstract calls Bermeo (Northern Bizkaian) Basque a lexical pitch accent language; de Rijk 1972 says that for Gipuzkoan Basque no stress-assignment rule was known, that prominence is weak and varies between villages, and that relativized verb forms take final stress. de Rijk's 1972 'no one knows the rules' is a statement about the state of knowledge then and is superseded by Hualde's later dialect-by-dialect work (1997, and the unopened 1999 survey), not a competing placement claim. The two Hualde chapters most likely to give a pan-dialectal statement (1999, 1993) could not be opened: their 'open copy' tags rest on WALS bibliographic records, not files.

sources.citation: Elordieta, Gorka & Elisabeth Selkirk (2018). Notes on prosodic headedness and tone in Tokyo Japanese, Standard English and Northern Bizkaian Basque. In Hana-bana: A Festschrift for Junko Ito and Armin Mester (UCSC, online). [Glottolog 612507]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: in NBB, there is a lexical contrast between accented and unaccented words, like in Tokyo Japanese. [...] In the particular variety of NBB on which we will base our analysis (the one of Lekeitio), main prosodic prominence is always found on a fixed syllable in an accented word, regardless of the location of that syllable with respect to the accented morpheme. This syllable is the penultimate of the whole word, which may consist of a bare root with no overt affix or a root plus one or more affixes. A falling accent HL surfaces on this penult syllable.
sources.locator: sec. 4 'Northern Bizkaian Basque', paragraphs before ex. (24) (the text layer)
sources.note: First-hand (Elordieta is the Lekeitio specialist): Northern Bizkaian Basque has a lexical accented/unaccented contrast; accented words carry a HL pitch accent on the penultimate syllable of the whole word (libúru 'book', liburuári, lagunári vs unaccented lagun, lagunena); unaccented words have no word-level prominence and cannot form a phonological phrase alone. Confirms the catalog's 'lexical' kind for a different (western) variety from the Zuberoan deciding passage; theoretical paper, not a survey.

sources.quote: 'In this system, unmarked stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the base, which is the stem in Roncalese and the word in Zuberoan (e.g., gízun, gizún-a, néska, alhába). There is a marked accentuation pattern in which stress falls on the last syllable (e.g., alhabá, neská, ardṹ, ah̃ái)... words bearing some monosyllabic suffixes ... and compounds whose second member is monosyllabic are also oxytones... a syllabic trochee built at the right edge of the base... The non-absolutive plural suffix -e- is also marked... it attracts stress (gizun-ék, gizun-ér; gizun-éna; gizon-éntako).'

sources.quote: Quotes Michelena: accent position 'regulated taking the last syllable of the word as the starting point. Oxitony is exceptional'; village data show ABS sg/pl penultimate (o-ó-o: ardíak, txakǘrrak, gizúnak; o-o-ó-o: putikúak, alhargǘnak) and proposes a two-level derivation (word accent on lexeme-final syllable, then phrase-level accent on the penult after affixation, with a-deletion yielding surface oxytones in -a stems, e.g. alhabá); acoustic part reports stressed syllables with higher F0 and longer duration than neighbours in each village.
